| 38 | Table 1 DEI-officer row vs. note ("sample of 554 large districts") | full-column denominators reproduce every cell and SD (e.g., 15.00% × 140 = 21.0; 13.64% × 242 = 33.0) | MISMATCH (denominator presentation) | row is not a rate among measured districts |
| 39 | Equation (1) (p. 6) vs. estimated models | β₅ used twice; DEI-missing indicator and size interaction absent | MISMATCH (notation) | Figure 2 and the 417% claim come from a model not written out |
| 40 | Abstract: triggers "increase the likelihood" vs. p. 6 "without establishing causation" | n/a | MISMATCH (wording) | causal verb in a descriptive design |
| 41 | 6,943 challenged books; 2,532 and 3,362 banned books; 12,290 BLM events; N = 554 DEI sample (pp. 5–6) | not tabulated | UNCHECKABLE | |
| 42 | Robustness, extensions, count models, student/district demographics (pp. 5, 6, 11; fn. 7) | Appendix A; Tables B1–B11; Figures B1–B3 | UNCHECKABLE | online supplement not available to this review |

*Density and length.* At about 11 pages of text, the paper is efficient. A time-constrained reader can get the evidence from Table 1, Tables 2–3 (cols. 2, 3, 5, 6), and Figure 2, plus the first paragraph of Analytical Results (p. 8) and the Anti-DEI Policies subsection (pp. 10–11). The historical Background (pp. 3–4) can be skimmed. The last two Discussion paragraphs (p. 12), on school openness and security, are speculative extensions and should be read that way.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's most lasting contribution is descriptive. It is the first population-wide, district-level count I know of for 2021–23 local anti-DEI activity. It links four nonprofit trackers (Ballotpedia, ALA, CRT Forward, PEN America) to all 12,897 regular districts and posts the linked file publicly. It shows that contentious elections and book challenges (13.3% and 5.5% of districts) were far more common than anti-CRT policies and book bans (1.1% and 1.9%) (p. 2, Table 1; p. 7). Its analytic claim is that county-level "racial status threat" triggers predict policies but not ideas. That claim holds up as a set of modest conditional correlations for policies, concentrated in above-median-size districts. It is weaker than the abstract suggests on three points: the ideas "null," the "community rather than district" conclusion, and the racial-threat mechanism.

**Strengths:**

- **A national descriptive census that the field did not have.** [checkable] The paper covers the full population of 12,897 regular districts with four outcome measures and hand-assigned LEAIDs (pp. 4–5). Data are posted on Harvard Dataverse (p. 12, note 1). The ideas-vs-policies contrast is concrete and quotable: 2,115 districts (16%) had either kind of anti-DEI idea, and 348 (3%) had any anti-DEI policy (p. 7; notes 5–6). Anti-DEI ideas appeared in all 50 states and policies in 44 (p. 7). [judgment] For many readers this map of where the fight happened (Figure 1, p. 7) will be more useful than the theory test.
- **A useful district profile that cuts against the popular image.** [checkable] Districts with ideas or policies were much larger than average: mean enrollment 12.5k–25.4k vs. 3.5k. They were more suburban, more educated, and more diverse, and had similar or lower Trump vote share than the average district (57.05 overall vs. 46.68–57.13) (p. 2, Table 1). [judgment] Local anti-DEI politics in 2021–23 was mostly a large, suburban, contested-district phenomenon, not a deep-red rural one. That finding is well supported and worth citing.
- **Evidence on sequencing.** [checkable] 77% of districts with a policy also had anti-DEI ideas, compared with 15% of other districts. Among the 62% of anti-CRT-policy districts that had contentious elections, the elections always came before the policy (p. 8). This is descriptive, but it is real evidence for an agenda-setting pipeline running from ideas to policy.
- **A theory with a checkable prediction.** [judgment] Hopkins's (2010) "politicized places" idea is that national rhetoric catches on where local change is visible. Applying it to school-district politics gives a falsifiable prediction, and the positive policy associations with county demographic change and BLM protests are consistent with it (p. 9, Table 3, cols. 2 and 5).
- **Clear statements of caution in the body.** [checkable] The paper says it does not establish causation (p. 6). It flags the DEI-officer measure as valid only for large districts (pp. 6, 10). It notes that the outcome data probably miss events (p. 12, note 3).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The abstract's language outruns the design.** [checkable] The abstract says RST triggers "increase the likelihood" of policy adoption, and p. 10 says demographic change "significantly raise[s] the probability." The design is a single cross-section of LPMs with state fixed effects, and p. 6 explicitly disclaims causation. [judgment] The most quotable claim is causal. The best-supported claim is associational.
- **Absolute magnitudes are small, and the headline relative figure is fragile.** [checkable] Base rates are 1.1% and 1.9% (Table 1). A BLM protest goes with about 0.5 pp (p. 11; Table 3 col. 2: 0.006, col. 5: 0.005, p < .10). The "417%" figure compares 3.1% with 0.6% for a 75th-percentile district: an absolute gap of 2.5 pp (p. 10). [judgment, from reading Figure 2d] The 0.6% baseline is a predicted value at zero change. Its 95% band appears to include zero, so the ratio is poorly pinned down. My own arithmetic, assuming the change variable is scaled as a proportion (the paper does not state its units), puts the no-interaction model's implied association at the median (40%) change at about 0.7 pp for anti-CRT policy and 1.0 pp for book bans (Table 3, cols. 2 and 5). That scaling matches the "typical district" curves in Figure 2c–d. The R² values also suggest that triggers and controls explain little beyond state fixed effects: 0.071 → 0.078 for anti-CRT and 0.143 → 0.153 for bans when controls are added (Table 3, cols. 1–2, 4–5).
- **The ideas "null" is neither clean nor null.** [checkable] For contentious elections, every trigger coefficient flips from positive to negative once covariates are added. % residents of color goes 0.343*** → −0.050, % change 0.148*** → −0.039*, and BLM 0.064*** → −0.018** (Table 2, cols. 1–2). The paper attributes the flip mainly to district size (p. 9). For book challenges, BLM stays *positive* and significant with controls (0.008*, Table 2 col. 5). That is larger in absolute terms than the BLM coefficient for book bans (0.005+, Table 3 col. 5). The change × size interaction for book challenges (0.016***, Table 2 col. 6) is the same size as for book bans (0.016***, Table 3 col. 6). Figure 2b shows large-district challenge probabilities rising with demographic change. The DEI-officer "policy backlash" trigger predicts contentious elections at +10 pp (0.100**, Table 2 col. 2; p. 10). [judgment] So "these triggers are unrelated to the circulation of anti-DEI ideas" (abstract) holds cleanly only for one of the two idea measures, with the triggers defined narrowly. It is also partly an association absorbed by district size rather than a null. District size is plausibly both a confounder and partly downstream of the same demographic growth, and the timing of the size measure is not clear in the main text (p. 6). That same variable produces the policy heterogeneity that anchors the headline.
- **The ideas/policies contrast is partly a contrast between data sources.** [checkable] Election conflicts come from Ballotpedia's daily news searches (p. 5). Book challenges come from ALA reports and media, *including public-library challenges matched to district geography* (p. 5). Policies come from CRT Forward and PEN America (p. 5). The election measure records "conflicts … regarding race, gender, or sexuality" (p. 5), which is contention and not necessarily anti-DEI in direction. [judgment] Detection by news coverage almost certainly rises with district size and media-market density, which undercuts the assumption in note 3 that missed events are unrelated to the independent variables. Ideas are measured with less district specificity than policies, so their weaker link to county triggers is not purely substantive.
- **"Community-level cultural conflicts rather than school-district-specific policies or conditions" is the paper's broadest claim and one of its least supported.** [checkable] The "district-specific policy" side rests on the DEI-officer measure. That measure comes from a Heritage Foundation collection limited to 554 districts of 15,000+ students, with missing values coded 0 plus a missing indicator (p. 6). The policy coefficients are imprecise: anti-CRT −0.016 (SE 0.026), 95% CI ≈ [−0.067, 0.035]; book bans −0.045 (SE 0.029), CI ≈ [−0.102, 0.012] (Table 3, cols. 2 and 5; my arithmetic). [judgment] That null cannot rule out backlash effects many times the base rate. Its point estimate for bans actually runs the other way. The "district conditions" side (district and student demographics attenuating results) sits in Appendix Tables B2–B3, which I could not review. "Cultural conflict" itself is never measured. The measured variables are county demographic change and BLM protests.
- **The mechanism is inferred, not observed, and the extension points elsewhere.** [checkable] The paper does not measure White residents' attitudes or perceived threat, or who pushed each policy. On p. 11, the paper reports no evidence that results are driven by Black residents. It reports that change in the foreign-born share is "strongly associated" with anti-DEI policies (Appendix Table B11, not available to me). [judgment] Anti-CRT and book-ban policies mostly target content about race, Black history, and LGBTQ topics. If growth in the immigrant population is doing the work, the finding looks more like Hopkins's original immigrant-threat result carried over to schools than like a general "racial status threat" story. The main text does not reconcile this with its framing, or with the robustness claim that results are "extremely consistent" when controlling for foreign-born share (p. 11). A related measurement issue: the 2010→2020 census change in "people of color" is affected by the Census Bureau's 2020 redesign of race question processing. The multiracial count rose sharply, partly for that reason (Census Bureau guidance; high confidence). I cannot tell from the main text whether this is addressed. It bears on how literally to read "demographic change."
- **Hopkins's national-salience half is untested.** [judgment] Politicized places is an *interaction* between local change and national salience over time. Here national salience is effectively constant across a 2021–23 cross-section, so only the local-change half is examined. The paper has dated elections and anti-CRT policies (p. 8) but does not use timing in the analysis.
- **Discussion and practice advice run ahead of the evidence.** [checkable] The small-district pattern (attenuated or negative slopes, Figure 2c–d) is explained with "know one's neighbor" and school-community contact (pp. 10–12). It is then turned into advice for districts to open their doors (p. 12). [judgment] None of this is tested. "Small" here means the 25th percentile of district enrollment (Figure 2 note, p. 10), so the finding is about very small districts, and "large" (75th percentile) is not especially large by U.S. standards.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for:** a population-wide descriptive picture of 2021–23 local anti-DEI activity. Ideas were far more common than policies: 13.3%/5.5% of districts vs. 1.1%/1.9% (Table 1, p. 2), or 2,115 vs. 348 districts (p. 7). Both were concentrated in larger, suburban, more-educated, more-diverse districts with no more Trump support than average (Table 1).
- **Cite it for:** ideas usually coming before policies. 77% of policy districts had anti-DEI ideas vs. 15% of others, and contentious elections always preceded anti-CRT policies where both occurred (p. 8).
- **Cite it for:** a conditional, non-causal association between county growth in residents of color (and BLM protests) and district anti-DEI policy adoption. The association is concentrated in above-median-size districts and is small in absolute terms: about 0.5–1 pp in a typical district, and 2.5 pp for a 75th-percentile district at median change (Table 3; p. 10; p. 11).
- **Cite it for:** a reusable, publicly posted linked dataset (note 1, p. 12) for follow-on work.
- **Do not cite it for:** RST triggers *causing* anti-DEI policies. The design is cross-sectional and the authors disclaim causation (p. 6).
- **Do not cite it for:** "417% higher likelihood" without the absolute numbers (3.1% vs. 0.6%, p. 10). The relative figure divides by an imprecise near-zero baseline.
- **Do not cite it for:** anti-DEI ideas being *unrelated* to local conditions. Election-conflict associations reverse sign under controls (Table 2 cols. 1–2), BLM positively predicts book challenges (Table 2 col. 5), book challenges share the size interaction (Table 2 col. 6), and DEI officers predict election conflicts (+10 pp).
- **Do not cite it for:** anti-DEI policies not being a backlash to district DEI policies. The only test uses a large-district-only measure with confidence intervals spanning several times the base rate (p. 6; Table 3).
- **Do not cite it for:** evidence of *racial* status threat as the psychological mechanism. No attitudes are measured, and the paper's own extension points to change in the immigrant population rather than the Black population (p. 11; Appendix B11 not available to me).
- **Do not cite it for:** small-district community ties buffering against anti-DEI policy, or for practice recommendations. These are untested interpretations (pp. 10–12).
- **Open questions:**
  - Do triggers predict the *transition* from ideas to policy, conditional on ideas being present? The paper's own pipeline framing suggests this analysis, but it is not reported.
  - Does the result survive a timing-based design using the dated elections and policies?
  - Do the associations differ between states with and without state-level anti-CRT or book laws? State fixed effects absorb levels only.
  - Is the driver race, immigration, or something correlated with county population growth?
  - Do patterns from the 2021–23 wave carry over to the post-2025 period, when anti-DEI pressure increasingly comes through state and federal channels?

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Novelty.* The paper's new element is scale plus linkage. Earlier public-facing reports it cites observed that contentious districts were diversifying quickly, but without a comparison group (Kingkade & Chiwaya, 2021; Pollock et al., 2022; p. 5). Prior quantitative work on nationalized school-board politics was single-state (Shah et al., 2024, Wisconsin; p. 6). This paper supplies the comparison group: every regular district in the country. It also separates four outcomes on two conceptual tiers. That is a genuine advance. The theoretical move, importing RST and politicized places into educational governance, is sensible but not deep. The paper tests only the local-change half of Hopkins's argument, and its operationalizations (county change in people of color, any BLM protest in the county, a DEI officer) are coarse proxies for "threat." BLM protests occurred in counties covering 74.7% of districts (Table 1). Once size and urbanicity are controlled, what that indicator still captures beyond "not a small rural county" is unclear.

*Is the ideas-vs-policies asymmetry the finding the paper says it is?* This is the crux for how the paper will be cited. The framing is that ideas spread nationally regardless of local conditions, while policy took hold only where national narratives met local triggers. The evidence for the first half comes almost entirely from contentious elections, and even there it is an association that reverses sign once district size and covariates enter (Table 2, cols. 1–2). Book challenges behave more like policies than the framing admits. BLM is positive and significant, and the change × size interaction (0.016***) matches book bans exactly (Table 2 col. 6 vs. Table 3 col. 6). There is no formal test that coefficients differ across outcomes. Comparing coefficients across outcomes with base rates ranging from 1.1% to 13.3% is also delicate: a 0.5 pp shift means very different things against 1.9% and 13.3%. A fairer summary: *after conditioning on district size and sociodemographics, county triggers are positively associated with rare policy outcomes and with book challenges in larger districts, and are slightly negatively associated with election contention.* That result is more interesting and less tidy than the one the paper states.

*Significance.* The question matters. Anti-CRT and book-ban policies had real reach, and knowing where they took hold is policy-relevant. At their credible strength, the findings should update readers in three ways. First, local anti-DEI *policy* was rare even at the 2021–23 peak. Second, it concentrated in large, growing, diversifying suburban-type districts rather than tracking partisanship alone. Trump vote share predicts anti-CRT policy (0.076***, Table 3 col. 2) but not book bans (0.021, col. 5). Third, "ideas everywhere, policies rarely" is a reasonable description of the period. These points should shape how researchers and journalists talk about the "anti-CRT wave." The findings do not establish that demographic threat *produces* policy, or that district DEI initiatives do not provoke backlash.

*Generalizability.* Within 2021–23 the coverage is excellent: the full population, not a sample (p. 6). Across time it is limited. The window covers the peak of local anti-CRT activity (anti-CRT policies peaked in fall 2021, p. 5). Since then, activity has shifted toward state statutes and, from 2025, federal executive action on DEI. Whether local-trigger dynamics still matter when policy comes from above is unknown. Across states, state fixed effects absorb level differences but not heterogeneity. Local action may substitute for or complement state laws, and Figure 1b shows policy districts clustered visibly (e.g., Florida's county-wide districts are almost entirely shaded). The main text does not show whether the results hold in states without state-level restrictions. The paper states its non-causal boundary clearly (p. 6). It is less careful about scope in the abstract and discussion, where the "community-level cultural conflicts" language and the practice advice generalize beyond what is estimated.

*Standing in the literature.* On its descriptive question (where anti-DEI ideas and policies occurred nationally in 2021–23), this is plausibly now the best available evidence, and the dataset will be reused. On its explanatory question (does local racial threat drive anti-DEI policy?), it is a first cross-sectional pass, not the reference answer. Work it does not engage that bears on its design choices includes the following (from my own knowledge, not cited in the paper):

- Enos (2014, *PNAS*): a field experiment showing that brief exposure to Spanish speakers shifted exclusionary attitudes. Enos (2017, *The Space Between Us*): on the geography of racial threat. Both are relevant to the choice of county as the unit of exposure. High confidence.
- Newman (2013, *AJPS*): on "acculturating contexts" and sudden change. Moderate–high confidence.
- Abrajano & Hajnal (2015, *White Backlash*): on immigration-driven White political reaction. High confidence. Directly relevant given the foreign-born result.
- Hopkins (2018, *The Increasingly United States*): on the nationalization of American politics. High confidence. Relevant to the paper's national-narrative framing.

*Follow-on work it sets up.* The most valuable next steps are:

1. Model policy adoption conditional on idea exposure, since the pipeline framing implies it.
2. Exploit the dated elections and policies (p. 8) in a timing design.
3. Link board-composition changes after contentious elections to subsequent policy.
4. Unpack immigration vs. race drivers in the main text, not the appendix.
5. Test the small-district "contact" hypothesis directly.
6. Study the downstream effects the discussion mentions but does not measure, such as teacher self-censorship and library acquisitions (p. 11, citing Slungaard Mumma, 2024).

*Limits of this review.* I did not have access to Appendix A or Appendix B (Tables B1–B11; Figures B1–B3). Several of the paper's supporting claims live there: district-level demographics attenuating results (B2–B3), DEI-officer robustness (B4–B8), and the foreign-born extension (B11). I have treated those claims as asserted, not verified.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (low confidence)

The paper uses only public or organization-shared data sources, names each one, and says in a data statement that "all data" are deposited on Harvard Dataverse (Note 1, p. 12). The headline model is a simple one: a linear probability model with state fixed effects and robust standard errors (p. 6), with full coefficient tables, N, and R² (Tables 2–3, pp. 8–9). With the analytic file in hand, a reader could probably re-run the main tables. From the PDF alone, however, the analytic dataset could not be rebuilt. The paper never mentions code, software, or the hand-coded LEAID crosswalks. The regressor scalings are not stated and sometimes contradict the labels. Several construction steps are described too loosely to follow: the county-to-district merge, the BLM timing rule, and how outcomes were matched to districts. Every robustness claim rests on an online appendix that I could not see. The rating is at the low end of Adequate, and it depends on the deposit containing the analytic file.

**Strengths:**

- [checkable] Every primary data source is named, with its coverage window. Ballotpedia contentious elections run January 2021–May 2023 (p. 5). ALA book challenges cover 2022 (p. 5). CRT Forward anti-CRT policies run August 2020–December 2023 (p. 5). The PEN America Book Bans Index covers 2021–22 and 2022–23 (p. 5). ACLED BLM events run May 24, 2020–March 1, 2023, with 12,290 events (p. 6). The paper also names the 2010/2020 decennial census, the Common Core of Data (CCD), MIT Election Lab 2016/2020 county returns, and the Heritage Foundation DEI-officer data (Greene, 2021; pp. 5–6).
- [checkable] There is a data availability statement pointing to a persistent DOI (https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/MZAWNA; Note 1, p. 12). By journal-era norms this counts in the paper's favor over "available upon request."
- [checkable] The estimator is simple and clearly named. The paper uses LPMs with state fixed effects and "robust standard errors" (p. 6). Each outcome gets three nested specifications: no controls, with controls, and with a change × logged district size interaction (Tables 2–3, cols 1–6). Every column reports N = 12,897, R², adjusted R², and standard errors (pp. 8–9).
- [checkable] The descriptive counts add up internally. Table 1 (p. 2) gives 1,718, 714, 140, and 242 districts out of 12,897 (13.3%, 5.5%, 1.1%, 1.9%). The union counts in the text also reconcile with the footnotes: 1,718 + 714 − 317 = 2,115 (p. 7, Note 5) and 140 + 242 − 34 = 348 (p. 7, Note 6). The headline book-ban contrast is arithmetically correct: 3.1% vs 0.6% is "417% greater" (p. 10), and it matches a reading of Figure 2d (p. 10).
- [checkable] Some missing-data handling is made explicit. The DEI-officer variable codes missing values as 0 and adds a missingness indicator (p. 6). Enrollment gaps are filled by linear interpolation from adjacent years (p. 6; details in Appendix A).

**Weaknesses:**

- [checkable] The regressor scaling is not documented, and the labels conflict with the coefficients.
  - Table 1 reports "% Residents of color" as a percent (mean 28.87, SD 19.26; p. 2). Table 2 col 1 gives a coefficient of 0.343 (p. 8), which is only plausible if the variable enters as a proportion (0–1). [judgment]
  - Trump vote share (Table 1 mean 57.05; Table 2 col 2 coefficient 0.132) and bachelor's share (mean 18.42; coefficient 0.836) show the same mismatch (pp. 2, 8).
  - "District % poverty" has a coefficient of −0.006 (SE 0.000; Table 2 col 2, p. 8). That fits a percent scale, and on a proportion scale it would be substantively trivial. So the scaling may not even be consistent across regressors. [judgment]
  - Median household income has no units in Table 1 (61.70, p. 2). Its coefficient of −0.001 (Table 2, p. 8) implies thousands of dollars, but the paper never says so.
  - The paper does not say whether logged district size is a natural log, what units enrollment is in before logging, or whether it is centered. These choices matter for the interaction columns and for Figure 2.
- [checkable] The key trigger, "% change in residents of color," is defined in three incompatible ways. Page 5 calls it "the change in the percentage of people of color between 2010 and 2020", which reads as a percentage-point change. Page 6 calls it "the percentage change since 2010." Page 10 calls it "growth rates." Its Table 1 mean of 45.42 (SD 33.92; p. 2) and the "median of demographic change (40%)" (p. 10) can only be relative growth rates [judgment], but the paper never says whether the growth is in the count or in the share of residents of color. It also doesn't say whether the quadratic term is the square of the same scaled variable.
- [checkable] Equation (1) (p. 6) does not match the estimated models.
  - The coefficient β5 is used for both BLM and DEI Officer.
  - DEI Officer has no *i* subscript.
  - The DEI-missing indicator is not in the equation and is not reported in Tables 2–3.
  - The size interaction in columns 3 and 6 is not written out, so it is unclear whether size also interacts with the quadratic term. The tables show only one interaction row (pp. 8–9).
  - Page 6 calls urbanicity "dichotomized," but the tables report two indicators, suburban and rural/town (pp. 8–9).
- [checkable] The outcome-to-district matching is manual and undocumented. LEAIDs were "hand-collected" for Ballotpedia by district name and state (p. 5). They were "manually assigned" for CRT Forward (p. 5). ALA public-library challenges were "matched" from library location to district (p. 5), with no stated boundary vintage and no rule for libraries whose service areas span several districts. For PEN America the paper describes no matching procedure at all (p. 5). No match rates, unmatched records, or ambiguous cases are reported anywhere. For example, the paper says "Ballotpedia identified 1,718 districts" (p. 5), and the analytic count is also 1,718 (Table 1, p. 2). A reader cannot tell whether that figure is before or after matching.
- [checkable] The BLM timing rule is not operational. A district counts as treated if its county had a protest "prior to any anti-DEI idea or policy" (p. 6). The paper says precise dates exist only for elections and anti-CRT policies (p. 8). Book challenges are dated only to the year 2022, and bans only to the academic year (p. 5). So "prior" is undefined for two of the four outcomes. The paper also doesn't say whether BLM is one variable or four outcome-specific variables, or what cutoff applies to districts with no anti-DEI event.
- [checkable] Several construction steps are deferred to Appendix A (not available to me):
  - the county-to-district merge using NCES geographic relationship files, including how multi-county districts are weighted (p. 5);
  - the enrollment interpolation (p. 6);
  - the "cross-sectional with measures of change" data structure (p. 6).

  The BLM variable uses "any district overlapping a county" (p. 6). It is unclear whether the demographic and Trump-share measures use the same rule or population weights. The Trump-share variable is an "average of these 2 years" (p. 6), with no statement of whether it is the share of total or two-party vote.
- [checkable] Some source descriptions are ambiguous or appear inaccurate.
  - Education, median household income, and poverty are attributed to the "2020 decennial census" (p. 6). To my knowledge, the 2020 decennial census does not collect income, education, or poverty. A replicator would have to guess at the actual product, most likely some American Community Survey tabulation. [judgment]
  - Poverty is called "the percentage of the district students in poverty" on p. 6 but "District % poverty" in Table 1 (p. 2). No source is named.
  - Library staff is not tied to any named source or year.
  - The robustness checks use an "American Ideology Project" measure (p. 11) that is neither described in the Data section nor in the reference list.
  - The acknowledgments thank the Brown Center on Education Policy for sharing data (p. 12), but no variable is attributed to it.
  - Apart from Greene (2021), none of the data sources has a formal reference entry, version, or access date.
- [checkable] The sample universe is not defined. "12,897 regular school districts" (p. 4) comes with no CCD agency-type code, year, or exclusion steps. Every model has N = 12,897 (Tables 2–3). That implies either no missing values on any covariate or imputation beyond the two documented cases, and the paper does not say which.
- [checkable] The DEI-officer frame is ambiguous. The data are "limited to districts with 15,000 students (N = 554)" (p. 6), with no threshold year and no ≥ or > stated. Table 1's note says the data come "from a sample of 554 large districts," but the all-district mean is 1.67% (SD 12.83; p. 2). That is roughly 215 districts if the denominator is 12,897 with missing values coded 0, or roughly 9 if the denominator is the 554. The table does not say which.
- [checkable] The paper states no software, package, version, or code availability. The standard-error type is only "robust" (p. 6), with no HC variant and no clustering. The main regressors are county-level and shared across districts, so the reported significance stars depend on a choice the paper does not discuss (substance deferred to the methods reviewers). [judgment]
- [checkable] Some exhibits cannot be regenerated from the paper's description, and some reported values are too imprecise to check.
  - Figure 2 (p. 10) plots predictions at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of size. The paper does not say how other covariates and the state fixed effects are held.
  - Income and poverty coefficients print as "−0.000 (0.000)" or "−0.001 (0.000)" (Tables 2–3). These values are uninformative.
  - With state fixed effects, the reported "Constant" depends on an unstated normalization.
  - I tried to reproduce the Figure 2d contrasts from the Table 3 col 6 coefficients and could not do it without guessing at the unstated scaling, log base, and centering. [judgment]

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before relying on the results, open the Dataverse deposit (Note 1, p. 12). Check whether it contains (a) the analysis code, (b) the district-level analytic file, and (c) the hand-coded LEAID crosswalks for Ballotpedia, ALA, CRT Forward, and PEN America. The paper does not say. If only raw source files are deposited, the analytic sample cannot be rebuilt as described. Also check whether ACLED and ALA records are redistributed or only derived indicators. The paper says ALA data were "provided by" ALA (p. 5), so readers probably cannot independently obtain the ALA inputs.
- If code exists, confirm these before interpreting magnitudes:
  - the 0–1 vs 0–100 scaling of each regressor;
  - whether "% change" is a percentage-point change or a growth rate, and of what (the count or the share);
  - the log base, units, and centering of district size;
  - income units;
  - which covariates are county-level vs district-level, and how multi-county districts are handled.

  Until then, treat the coefficient sizes in Tables 2–3 as uninterpretable without the figure. Treat Figure 2 as the only interpretable effect-size display, and note that it too rests on unstated prediction settings.
- Ask for, or reconstruct, the match rates for each of the four outcome sources. Also ask how the BLM "prior to any anti-DEI idea or policy" rule (p. 6) was applied to year-dated outcomes. Outcome-dependent coding of the regressor is the step most likely to change results under a faithful replication.
- An easy first check: re-estimate Table 3 cols 2 and 5 with county-clustered standard errors. The BLM coefficients (0.006, SE 0.002, and 0.005, SE 0.003; Table 3, p. 9) and the ideas results in Table 2 are the most likely to lose significance if clustering matters.
- Treat the following as unverifiable from the article alone. Each rests entirely on online Appendix B tables and figures that are not in the PDF:
  - the robustness claims on p. 11 (Tables B4–B8: foreign-born control, violent vs nonviolent BLM, anti-CRT-only elections, 2020-only Trump share, American Ideology Project, no DEI officer, the DEI-nonmissing sample);
  - the claim on p. 6 that the DEI-officer coding "do[es] not affect the overall results" (B4–B8);
  - the county- vs district-demographics argument (B2–B3, p. 5);
  - the count models (B1, Figure B1; p. 5, Note 7);
  - the immigrant extension (B11, p. 11);
  - the nonlinearity justification (Figure B2, p. 6).

  Two further claims cite no exhibit at all: that the sign change in Table 2 is "primarily driven by accounting for district size" (p. 9), and that results are "not sensitive" to the two 2020 CRT policies (Note 4, p. 12). Figure B3 is also cross-referenced inconsistently: p. 9 describes it as the ideas visualization, and p. 10 cites it as the policies visualization.
- Read the DEI-officer coefficients (e.g., 0.100 in Table 2 col 2, p. 8) as coming from a missing→0 coding that holds only for the 554 large districts. Here the reproducibility and validity caveats overlap, and the paper itself urges caution (p. 6, p. 10).

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Data availability.* The paper does better than much of this literature on the most basic point: it names its sources and posts a DOI-linked deposit (Note 1, p. 12). All inputs are either public (Census, CCD, MIT Election Lab, PEN America index, CRT Forward, the Heritage report, and Ballotpedia's web listings) or shared by the originating organization (ALA; acknowledgments, p. 12). None of them is a restricted-use administrative file, so the usual excuse for limited sharing does not apply here. The online supplement (Appendix A, data details; Appendix B, Tables B1–B11 and Figures B1–B3) was not available to me. I could not check the deposit either, since I was not permitted to fetch it. What I can say is that the article text never mentions code, software, or a README. The deposit is described only as holding "data." Journal-era norms would expect a replication package or a stated reason there is none, and the article provides neither.

*Rebuilding the analytic file.* A replicator starting from the raw sources would have to guess at eight or so steps:

1. how the 12,897-district universe was defined in the CCD (p. 4);
2. the name-and-state crosswalks for Ballotpedia and CRT Forward, and the unexplained match for PEN America (p. 5);
3. the library-location-to-district assignment for ALA (p. 5);
4. the weighting in the county-to-district merge, deferred to Appendix A (p. 5);
5. the BLM timing rule, which is undefined for the two year-dated outcomes (pp. 5–6, 8);
6. the scale and definition of the change variable, which is described three different ways (pp. 5, 6, 10);
7. the actual source of the income, education, and poverty data (p. 6);
8. the enrollment interpolation (p. 6).

Every one of these involves researcher judgment, and none has a reported diagnostic such as a match rate or the number of imputed values. The outcome variables are the product of manual record linkage, so this is where replication risk is concentrated. Footnote 3 (p. 12) assumes that missed events are unrelated to the regressors. That assumption covers the source organizations' coverage, not the authors' own matching error.

*Specification.* The estimator is transparent, and the three-column structure is easy to follow. The obstacle to re-running from the text is scaling, not model choice. The coefficient magnitudes show that the table's "%" labels do not match the units in the regressions (Table 1 vs Tables 2–3). Equation (1) has a duplicated β5 and omits both the missingness indicator and the interaction term (p. 6). Given the analytic file and code, these problems disappear. Given only the PDF, a reader would have to reverse-engineer them, and my attempt to recover Figure 2d from the Table 3 col 6 coefficients did not pin down the unknowns.

*Results reporting.* The main tables are complete in the conventional sense: coefficients, SEs, N, R², and adjusted R², for all 12 models (pp. 8–9). Some precision is lost to three-decimal rounding on the income and poverty rows. The descriptive counts reconcile internally (Table 1; Notes 5–6). Beyond Tables 2–3 and Figure 2, however, much of the paper's claim structure rests on material outside the article: the robustness section, the choice of county-level measurement, the count-model corroboration, and the foreign-born extension. The sequencing claims on p. 8 ("77%" vs "15%"; 62% of anti-CRT districts had prior contentious elections, which "always preceded" the policies) cite no exhibit beyond the bivariate Table B9. For a reader who has only the article, the verifiable core is Tables 2–3 and Figure 2. Everything else is taken on trust pending the supplement and the deposit.

*Bottom line.* This is not a case where missing documentation hides the central result. The design is simple, the sources are public, and a deposit is claimed. That is why the rating is Adequate and not Weak. But the article by itself is not a replication document. Whether the findings are verifiable depends on what sits at the Dataverse DOI, and readers should check that before citing specific magnitudes.
